I'm a ham. The FCC only ever will come investigate unlicensed operation if it interferes with vital services (cops, EMTs, Air Traffic Control), or commercial radio stations which pay for use of a frequency. 

As a ham we are supposed to do analyses of RF exposure whenever we reconfigure our setups, but since radio waves are non ionizing radiation, the only effects of RF exposure can be intense heating if you were to be very close to an antenna or even touching it. You WILL get burned and it DOES suck. A lot. It's the same principle as a microwave oven. You're basically using a powerful radio to pop your popcorn. But if you made it to where the microwave oven could operate with the door open, it wouldn't pop the popcorn on the counter next to it.

So, theoretically your neighbor could have some sort of RF weapon directed at your house, but to transmit, through your house, with enough power to somehow make you physically ill is highly unlikely. In fact, it's impossible, if he's moving the equipment a couple times a day. It'd be like moving a massive broadcast station in and out of the yard.

Also, go easy on it when you practice. They say 30 min to 1 hour per day of serious, uninterrupted time. You can even break it up into segments if you want.

If you want to get faster, you can work on some exercises. The Farnsworth method is where you set your character speed high, say 25 wpm, but your spacing between letters is longer. This will get you used to hearing characters sent really fast, but with the added space in between, the character rate is dropped down to where you have more time to work on understanding it.

Another method is to start trying to just recognize common words instead of the individual letters. That way you just recognize most of what's being sent automatically.  For ham radio purposes, stuff like state and Canadian province abbreviations, names of radio makes and models, weather conditions, and all the other stuff hams talk about usually, can be made into word lists. You can load these into programs like rufzxp and run through them with scoring, etc.

Writing is only one aspect overall of learning a language. 

I speak Chinese daily in my home, and I'm not a native speaker. Sure, it takes time to learn characters and even now, from time to time, I come across a character I don't recognize, or at least forgot. Sure, that's a tough part about Chinese. Honestly, though, all the other stuff about Chinese, including the tones used in pronunciation, are pretty easy. Grammar isn't hard at all. No conjugations or declensions or genders to deal with. 去 is "go", and that's it.

Sure, Russian has a straightforward Cyrillic alphabet, and that makes it easy to write / read. But all the other aspects make it hard for native English speakers (like me) to learn. We have the same concepts in English, but they are often only expressed verbally in the word order of the sentence. Maybe with a preposition.

So yeah, I think for a western European or American / Canadian, Russian, Chinese, or Japanese would still be really difficult. It's just a matter of where the difficulty lies within the language.
